To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the induction of hyperplastic nodular lesions in rat liver by 2-FA and CCl4 can be used as a short-term in situ assay for both initiating and promoting activity in vivo.

the short-term in vivo assay based on induction of hyperplastic nodular lesions in rat liver is a sensitive, rapid and cost-effective means to screen chemicals for both initiating and promoting activities.
short-term in vivo assay systems can be used to distinguish between carcinogens and non-carcinogen and to classify carcinogens into 2 major categories, hepatocarcino- gens and non-hepatocarcongens.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a short-term in vitro and in vivo assay system for carcinogenicity.
the development of a short-term in vitro assay system for detecting the carcinogenic activity of chemicals and with the application of this system in screening chemicals for carcinogenicity.
the development of an in vivo short-term assay system for detecting both initiating and promoting activity of chemicals in a single animal.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the initiation-promotion model for carcinogenesis in the rat is a valid system for the evaluation of the carcinogenic potential of chemicals in vivo.
our in vivo assay system is a useful short-term assay for both initiating and promoting activities.
the results of this study support the hypothesis that the initiation-promotion process is a general mechanism of chemical carcinogenesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a chemical carcinogen can be defined as a chemical which has initiating and enhancing (i.e., promoting) activity, whereas a non-carcinogen does not have these activities.

a positive response in our assay system for initiating activity is an indication of a carcinogen and a positive response in the assay system for enhancing (promoting activity) is an indication of the potential for a carcinogen.
the in vivo short-term assay system for carcinogenic activity is more sensitive and more discriminating than the in vitro short-term assay systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the initiation-promotion model for carcinogenesis in the liver of the rat is an excellent system for screening chemicals for carcinogenicity.
the initiation-promotion assay is an effective means of assessing the carcinogenic potential of chemicals.
a combination of in vitro and in vivo assays can provide more information about carcinogenic potential of test chemicals than can in vitro assays alone.
